passages.happening:
“The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth—and not I alone, but also all who know the truth— because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever” (verses 1-2).

“Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and love” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The letter opens the way ordinary letters did in that world: the sender, the readers, a greeting. But each part is filled with the faith.

The sender calls himself simply ‘the elder’. The word can mean an older man or a church leader. Here it seems to be a title everyone knew. Early Christians named him as John, and the letter's words are very close to 1 John's.

The readers are ‘the chosen lady and her children’. Many readers take the lady as a picture of a local church, with its members as her children, and her ‘elect sister’ at the end as the elder's own church. Others think she was a real woman, perhaps one who hosted a church in her house. The Greek word for lady, kuria, was also used as a name.

Notice the word ‘truth’, three times in two verses. The elder loves these people ‘in the truth’, and so do all who know it. Truth is not only a set of correct statements. It ‘abides in us and will be with us forever’. It is God's reality, shown in Christ, living in believers and binding them together.

The greeting is fuller than usual: grace, mercy and peace. They come from the Father and from ‘Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father’, side by side. And they come ‘in truth and love’, the two words the whole letter holds together.
passages.ot:
The blessing of grace and peace echoes the priests' blessing in Israel: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24-26).

And truth that lasts forever is the psalm's praise: “For great is His loving devotion toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever” (Psalm 117:2).
passages.hard:
Who is ‘the chosen lady’? Was she a real woman or a church?

Readers have taken her both ways, and both readings have ancient and modern defenders. These notes do not choose.

Many take her as a picture of a local church. They point out that the elder speaks of ‘some of your children’ as if of a congregation, that the warnings fit a whole church, and that the New Testament can picture God's people as a woman: a mother (Galatians 4:26) or a bride (Revelation 21:2). On this reading, ‘the children of your elect sister’ (verse 13) are the members of another church.

Others think she was a real Christian woman, perhaps the head of a household where a church met. Lydia opened her house to Paul (Acts 16:15), and a church met in Nympha's house (Colossians 4:15). The word kuria was also a personal name, and a few readers have suggested reading it that way.

On either reading, the letter is written to a household of faith, and its love and its warnings are for a whole church.
passages.asks: Ask whom you love ‘in the truth’, and what binds you to them. Ask what it means for you that truth ‘will be with us forever’. And ask whether grace, mercy and peace sound to you like a formula, or a gift you need today.

passages.happening:
“I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father has commanded us” (verse 4).

“And now I urge you, dear lady—not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning—that we love one another. And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
The elder begins with joy. He has found ‘some of your children walking in the truth’. Whether ‘some’ means that only some were, or simply that he had met some of them, is not clear. Either way, he starts with what is good.

‘Walking’ is a picture of a whole way of life, step by step. Truth is not only something to believe. It is a road to walk.

Then he asks for one thing: ‘that we love one another’. It is not new. They have had it ‘from the beginning’, from the first time they heard the gospel. Jesus gave it to his disciples on the night before he died.

And then the elder defines love, and his definition may surprise. ‘This is love, that we walk according to His commandments.’ Love is not a feeling set against God's commands. It is the life those commands describe. And the command, in turn, is to walk in love. The two make a circle. Love keeps the commands; the commands call for love.

That circle matters for the warning that comes next. The elder's love does not make him careless about the truth, and his care for the truth does not make him unloving.
passages.ot:
The command to love goes back to the law: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

And the law already joined love and obedience: “You shall therefore love the LORD your God and always keep His charge, His statutes, His ordinances, and His commandments” (Deuteronomy 11:1).

Walking in God's ways is the psalms' picture of a whole life: “Direct me in the path of Your commandments, for there I find delight” (Psalm 119:35).
passages.asks: Ask whether the people who know you best would say you walk in the truth. Ask whether you think of God's commands as the opposite of love, or as its shape. And ask whom you are finding it hard to love, and what the oldest command asks of you there.

passages.happening:
“For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist” (verse 7).

“Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded. Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Now the warning. ‘Many deceivers have gone out into the world.’ These are the same kind of people 1 John describes: teachers who had left the fellowship (1 John 2:19) and were now travelling from church to church. The word for deceiver means one who leads others astray, off the road.

Their error is named exactly: ‘refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh’. They seem to have taught that the divine Christ did not truly and lastingly become human, perhaps that he only seemed to have a body. For the elder this is not a small difference of opinion. If the Son of God did not truly come in the flesh, he did not truly die for anyone.

‘Watch yourselves.’ The elder does not want the church to lose what has been built. And he names the deceivers' appeal. They ‘run ahead’. They seem to have offered a more advanced faith, beyond what the church had first received. The elder says that going beyond Christ is not progress. It is losing God. ‘Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son.’

‘The teaching of Christ’ may mean the teaching about Christ, or the teaching Christ himself gave. Both fit.
passages.ot:
The law warned against prophets who led people away from the true God, even if they did signs: “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the LORD your God is testing you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

And Jeremiah spoke of prophets who offered new visions of their own: “They are filling you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16).

The call to hold to what was first given is the prophets' too: “Stand at the crossroads and look. Ask for the ancient paths: ‘Where is the good way?’ Then walk in it” (Jeremiah 6:16).
passages.hard:
Who is ‘the deceiver and the antichrist’? Is the elder speaking of one person at the end of the world?

In these letters the word ‘antichrist’ is used of people the readers could meet. 1 John says that ‘many antichrists have appeared’ and that the antichrist is ‘the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ’ (1 John 2:18, 22). Here the elder says that any teacher who denies the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh ‘is the deceiver and the antichrist’. The word describes what such a teacher is and does.

Many Christians also expect a final figure of evil before Christ returns, and link John's word with Paul's ‘man of lawlessness’ (2 Thessalonians 2:3) and the beast of Revelation. Others read those passages as speaking of a power of rebellion that takes shape again and again. The notes on 2 Thessalonians 2 set out the readings.

Over the centuries people have often named someone of their own day as the antichrist, or tied the figure to an emperor, a pope, a sultan or a dictator. Such identifications have been made many times, and they have often frightened believers and turned Christians against one another. These notes make none. They identify the antichrist with no living person, office, church, nation, leader or movement. The elder's own use points elsewhere: test every teacher by what he confesses about Jesus Christ come in the flesh.
passages.asks: Ask what you believe about Jesus, and whether it is the Jesus who truly came in the flesh. Ask whether you have been drawn to a teaching that promises something more advanced than Christ. And ask what it would mean for you to ‘remain’ in his teaching this week.

passages.t: ‘Do not receive him into your home’
passages.happening: “If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
These two verses need to be read in their own world.

The early church spread through hospitality. Travelling teachers, prophets and missionaries moved from town to town and relied on believers to house and feed them and send them on. Churches met in homes. So to receive a travelling teacher ‘into your home’ was to receive him into the house church: to give him a hearing in that congregation and a kind of endorsement.

The ‘greeting’ the elder has in mind was most likely the formal welcome and blessing given to a guest teacher. It said, in effect, ‘we stand with you and your message’. That is why the elder says that whoever gives it ‘shares in his evil deeds’. To bless and send on a teacher who denies that Jesus Christ came in the flesh would make the church his partner in spreading that teaching.

The teachers in view are specific. They are the deceivers of verse 7, who deny Christ's coming in the flesh, and who come looking for a base for their work.
passages.ot:
Hospitality to travellers runs deep in the Old Testament. Abraham ran to meet three strangers at his tent and begged them, “please do not pass your servant by” (Genesis 18:3). The law commanded love for the stranger: “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).

But the law also warned against giving a hearing to those who would lead Israel to other gods: “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer” (Deuteronomy 13:3). 2 John keeps both: a wide welcome for people, and no platform for a false Christ.
passages.hard:
Does this mean Christians should refuse to greet or welcome people who believe differently, even family members, neighbours or people of other faiths?

No. In its setting the instruction is narrow. It concerns travelling teachers who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, and who came seeking a church's hospitality as a base for their teaching. To receive them into the house church and give them the customary blessing would be to share in their work.

Christians apply the principle in different ways. Some apply it to any teacher who denies central Christian truth, such as the deity or the humanity of Christ. Others stress that it concerns a church's public sponsorship of a teacher, not ordinary courtesy to individuals, and they note that the same letter commands love. Few think it forbids kindness to unbelievers, conversation with doubters, or hospitality to those who differ on smaller questions. These notes do not choose between those applications.

But the verses are not a licence to shun family members, neighbours, or people of other faiths. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners. Believers are to be friends, neighbours, coworkers and good citizens with people of every faith and none. Nothing here gives anyone a reason to look down on unbelievers.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask how your church decides whom to give a platform to, and what it would look like to be both open-handed and careful. Ask whether you have used verses like these to keep away people you simply disagreed with. And ask whom you could welcome this week.

passages.happening:
“I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete” (verse 12).

“The children of your elect sister send you greetings” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends warmly. The elder has more to say, but not on paper. He hopes to come and speak ‘face to face’.

Ancient letters often said something like this. Writing was a second-best substitute for being there. Letters were written on sheets of papyrus with reed pens and ink, and a short letter like this one would fit on one sheet.

‘So that our joy may be complete.’ 1 John began with the same hope (1 John 1:4). For the elder, love and truth are not only things to argue for. They are shared, in person, and they make joy full.

The last line sends greetings from ‘the children of your elect sister’. If the lady is a church, this is the church where the elder is, sending love to a sister church. If she is a woman, these are her sister's children. Either way, the letter ends where it began: with a family.
passages.ot:
The hope of meeting face to face recalls how God spoke with Moses: “the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11).

And the joy of God's people gathered together is the psalm's: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1).
passages.asks: Ask whom you need to speak to face to face rather than in writing. Ask what makes your joy ‘complete’. And ask which sister church or Christian friend you could send a word of love to this week.
